statement: Locking collateral for the life of a tokenized derivatives contract raises participation, because investors prefer contracts whose collateral cannot be withdrawn early.
explanation: Locked collateral creates opportunity costs that may discourage investors from using tokenized trades.
originalText: Counterparty risk is mitigated, and participation rises, because investors prefer contracts whose collateral cannot be withdrawn early.

statement: Tokenization can make debt cheaper to issue than conventional bonds, which makes borrowing more attractive and can encourage higher leverage, raising the risk of instability in an interconnected system.
explanation: Cheaper debt, more borrowing, more leverage and more fragility is the channel. In a highly interconnected system, excessive debt raises the risk of instability.
originalText: Debt becomes cheaper to issue than conventional bonds, borrowing grows more attractive, and higher leverage can raise instability.

statement: Cheaper tokenized debt issuance lowers bank leverage and so reduces the risk of contagion.
explanation: Cheaper debt makes borrowing more attractive and can encourage higher leverage, not lower.
originalText: Debt becomes cheaper to issue, firms replace bank loans with bonds, and bank leverage falls, which reduces the risk of contagion.

statement: Tokenization makes debt costlier to issue than conventional bonds.
explanation: Tokenization can lower the issuance cost of debt compared with conventional bonds. Security spending is a separate infrastructure channel.
originalText: Debt becomes costlier to issue because of security spending, borrowing falls, and lower leverage slows the spread of shocks.
correction: Tokenization makes debt cheaper to issue than conventional bonds.

statement: Tokenization makes equity cheaper to issue relative to debt, so firms shift toward equity funding and leverage falls.
explanation: The mechanism is cheaper debt issuance, which raises leverage rather than lowering it.
originalText: Equity becomes cheaper to issue relative to debt, firms shift toward equity funding, and lower leverage dampens shock transmission.

statement: Tokenization can make it easier for retail investors to place funds in financial assets outside bank deposits, so banks may see retail deposits fall and rely more on wholesale funding that can dry up quickly in stress.
explanation: Wholesale funding can dry up in market stress, raising the risk of defaults and spillovers. This channel works through funding liquidity.
originalText: Retail deposits fall as funds move into financial assets, so the bank leans on wholesale funding that can dry up in stress.

statement: Tokenization raises bank retail deposits, because tokenized deposits become more attractive, so banks can rely less on wholesale funding.
explanation: The reading has retail deposits declining as funds move into financial assets.
originalText: Retail deposits rise as tokenized deposits become more attractive, so the bank can rely less on wholesale funding.

statement: A bank that loses retail deposits and replaces them with wholesale funding becomes more stable, because wholesale funding is less prone than deposits to run in stress.
explanation: Wholesale funding is the funding that can dry up quickly in stress, so greater reliance on it raises fragility.
originalText: Retail deposits fall, but the bank becomes more stable, because wholesale funding is less prone than deposits to run in stress.

statement: Tokenization leaves bank retail deposits unaffected, because it changes how securities settle rather than where households keep funds.
explanation: The reading explicitly links tokenization to retail funds moving out of bank deposits.
originalText: Retail deposits are unaffected, because tokenization changes how securities settle rather than where households keep funds.

statement: On shared, programmable ledgers, rehypothecation and the quick, cheap movement of funds across linked assets mean that a fall in one asset can set off rapid selloffs in several markets.
explanation: Interconnectedness that improves access also speeds up contagion and makes it harder for regulators to respond.
originalText: Rehypothecation and quick, cheap movement of funds across linked assets mean a fall in one asset can set off rapid selloffs in several markets.

statement: The reuse of the same collateral across several transactions is escrow certification.
explanation: Reusing collateral across transactions is rehypothecation. Escrow certificates belong to the common ledger model.
originalText: Reusing collateral across transactions is escrow certification, so each product is backed by an original asset locked on a separate ledger.
correction: The reuse of the same collateral across several transactions is rehypothecation.

statement: Linking products to other assets slows the transmission of shocks, because losses on one asset are offset by gains on the assets to which it is pegged.
explanation: Linked assets let shocks spread more rapidly, and the reading describes no offsetting effect.
originalText: Linked products slow the transmission of shocks, because losses on one asset are offset by gains on the assets to which it is pegged.

statement: A chain of self-executing smart contracts can set off large volumes of trades and contribute to a flash crash, and faster execution makes such shocks harder for policymakers to contain.
explanation: Programmable ledgers allow automated trading at much faster speeds, and faster transaction speeds make it more difficult for policymakers to contain the costs of externalities.
originalText: A chain of self-executing smart contracts set off large volumes of trades, and faster execution makes such shocks harder to contain.

statement: Smart contracts pause automatically in volatile markets, so sharp price falls on tokenized markets must reflect human order-entry errors.
explanation: Smart contracts execute as coded. Chained, self-executing contracts triggering large volumes of trades is the reading's mechanism for flash crashes.
originalText: Smart contracts pause automatically in volatile markets, so the fall must reflect human order-entry errors rather than automated trading.

statement: If the private operator of a dominant tokenized ledger underinvests in operational security, the resulting risks can affect all participants, and a single point of failure could disrupt the whole market.
explanation: The operator decides the spending but everyone bears the failure, which is an externality. The impact of failures grows with the number of users and interconnected transactions.
originalText: The board member is wrong: underinvestment creates risks for every participant, and one point of failure could disrupt the market.

statement: The potential impact of a failure of a tokenized ledger falls as more users join, because a larger ledger spreads losses more thinly.
explanation: The potential impact of failures grows with the number of users and interconnected transactions, so operators must spend more on security.
originalText: The board member is right: the impact of a failure falls as more users join, because a larger ledger spreads losses more thinly.

statement: Underinvestment in operational security by a ledger operator is a knowledge externality, because rival ledgers can copy the operator's code for free.
explanation: Knowledge externalities concern innovation spreading through open code. Underinvestment in security is an infrastructure externality, with risks falling on all participants.
originalText: The board member is wrong: security spending is a knowledge externality, because rival ledgers can copy the operator’s code for free.

statement: Even positive externalities can be socially inefficient: network effects on a tokenized ledger improve liquidity as users join, yet participation may stay below the socially optimal level.
explanation: Positive is not the same as optimal. The benefit a new user brings to others does not enter that user's own decision, so participation can fall short.
originalText: Even positive externalities can be ineﬀicient: liquidity improves as users join, yet participation may stay below the social optimum.

statement: Network effects on tokenized ledgers are a negative externality.
explanation: Network effects are the reading's example of a positive externality, because liquidity improves as more participants join.
originalText: Network effects on tokenized ledgers are negative, because each new user adds congestion, so participation tends to exceed the optimum.
correction: Network effects on tokenized ledgers are a positive externality.

statement: Network effects on a tokenized ledger are an internality, because each user's decision to join affects only that user's own liquidity.
explanation: An internality is a participant acting against its own interest. Network effects spill over to other users.
originalText: Network effects are an internality, because each user’s decision to join affects only that user’s own liquidity, so no optimum applies.

statement: Because network effects on a tokenized ledger are a positive externality, participation will reach the socially optimal level without any policy action.
explanation: Even positive externalities can lead to socially inefficient outcomes, and participation may remain below the social optimum.
originalText: The economist is right, because each new user raises liquidity for all users, which gives every potential user a private reason to join.

statement: When several non-interoperable tokenized ledgers coexist, liquidity splits into segmented pools, search frictions and transaction costs rise, and network externalities weaken.
explanation: The strength of network externalities depends on the interoperability of ledgers. The risk is greater when private entities set up ledgers without coordination or regulatory requirements for interoperability.
originalText: Liquidity splits into segmented pools, search frictions and transaction costs rise, and network externalities weaken.

statement: Smart contracts can run only where a single ledger serves the whole of the market.
explanation: Programmability depends on the design of each ledger, not on interoperability between ledgers.
originalText: Programmability falls on each ledger, because smart contracts can run only where one ledger serves the whole of the market.

statement: Competition among uncoordinated, non-interoperable tokenized ledgers deepens liquidity and narrows bid-ask spreads on every platform.
explanation: Segmentation reduces liquidity and raises transaction costs and search frictions.
originalText: Liquidity improves, because competition among the ledgers deepens each pool and narrows bid-ask spreads on every platform.

statement: Some intermediaries already offer fractional shares of certain equities, and tokenization extends fractional ownership to a wider range of assets, including bonds.
explanation: The novelty is breadth, not existence. When the issuer issues the tokens, intermediary risks can be reduced or even eliminated, improving access for smaller investors.
originalText: Some intermediaries already offer fractional shares of certain equities; tokenization extends this to more assets, including bonds.

statement: On tokenized ledgers, fractional ownership is still limited to equities.
explanation: Tokenization enables fractionalisation across a wider range of assets, including equities and bonds.
originalText: On tokenized ledgers, fractional ownership is still limited to equities, so the gain for small investors is lower fees, not wider access.

statement: Fractionalisation through tokens issued by the issuer raises intermediary risk for small investors.
explanation: Tokens issued directly by the issuer can reduce or even eliminate intermediary risks.
originalText: Fractionalisation raises intermediary risk for small investors, because tokens issued by the issuer add a layer between investor and asset.
correction: Fractionalisation through tokens issued by the issuer reduces intermediary risk for small investors.

statement: Fractionalisation leaves small investors less diversified.
explanation: Fractionalisation helps investors diversify. Insufficient diversification is the reading's consequence of bypassing advisers, not of fractionalisation.
originalText: The claim is right, but fractionalisation leaves small investors less diversified, which is the internality that the reading warns about.

statement: Open code on tokenized ledgers lets others build on existing smart contracts at low or no cost, but easy copying weakens the incentive to fund significant R&D.
explanation: Knowledge externalities grow as the platform's user base grows. Code can be quickly copied and improved by others, so incentives may hold up only if the shared user base is large enough.
originalText: Open code lets others build on existing smart contracts at low or no cost, but easy copying weakens the incentive to fund R&D.

statement: Knowledge externalities on a tokenized ledger shrink as its user base grows.
explanation: Knowledge externalities grow as the number of platform users increases.
originalText: Knowledge externalities shrink as the ledger’s user base grows, because more users mean more competitors copying each application.
correction: Knowledge externalities on a tokenized ledger grow as its user base grows.

statement: Because deployed smart contracts are immutable they cannot be copied, which means open code strengthens the incentive to invest in R&D.
explanation: Deployed smart contracts are immutable, but open code can still be copied and improved, which is the source of the weaker R&D incentive.
originalText: Smart contracts are immutable and so cannot be copied, which means open code strengthens the incentive to invest in R&D.

statement: Licensing and patenting widen the benefits of open-source development, because protected code can be shared more freely.
explanation: Licensing and patenting protect innovations but limit the benefits of open-source development.
originalText: Licensing and patenting widen the benefits of open-source development, because protected code can be shared more freely.
